items.stem: Explain why poverty increases vulnerability to hazards.
items.answer: Poor people live in hazardous locations and weak housing, lack savings and insurance, have poor access to warnings, health care and transport, and recover slowly.

items.stem: Explain the factors that influence hazard perception.
items.answer: Experience of past events; education and awareness; wealth and ability to act; religious and cultural beliefs; media; time since the last event; attachment to place.

Risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity. (a) Suggest two ways of increasing the capacity score of the highest-risk settlement. (b) Suggest limitations of using scores in the risk equation.
items.answer: (a) Evacuation plans and drills; warning sirens linked to the volcano observatory; trained local response teams; access roads; savings and insurance schemes. (b) Scores are subjective; factors are not independent; they combine very different variables; the hazard varies with eruption type.

items.stem: “Vulnerability is more important than the physical hazard in determining the scale of a disaster.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to magnitude, PAR model and development.
items.answer: For: Similar hazards cause very different losses: Haiti 2010 (M7.0, over 200 000 deaths) vs Christchurch 2011 (M6.2, 185 deaths); PAR model. Against: Extreme magnitude events overwhelm even prepared societies (Tōhoku 2011); the type and speed of onset of the hazard matter; some hazards are inherently deadly. Conclusion: Vulnerability usually explains differences in losses, though very large events cause disasters even where vulnerability is low.

items.stem: Explain the risk equation.
items.answer: Risk depends on the magnitude and frequency of the hazard multiplied by people’s vulnerability, divided by their capacity to cope; reducing vulnerability or increasing capacity reduces risk even if the hazard is unchanged.

items.stem: Explain how volcanic eruptions can be predicted.
items.answer: Monitoring of seismic swarms, ground deformation (tiltmeters, GPS, InSAR), gas emissions (SO₂), temperature changes and past eruption history; allowed the evacuation of over 60 000 people before Pinatubo in 1991.

items.stem: Explain the stages of Park’s disaster response curve.
items.answer: Normal quality of life; the event causes a sharp fall; relief (hours to days: rescue, medical care, aid); rehabilitation (weeks to months: services restored); reconstruction (years), possibly to a better level than before.

items.answer: Economic losses, homes and crops destroyed, people displaced, injuries, salinisation of land and long-term poverty also measure impact.

items.stem: Assess the view that preparedness is more effective than response in reducing the impacts of hazards.
items.answer: For: Warnings, drills, shelters and building codes save lives before an event (Bangladesh, Japan, Chile 2010); every dollar spent on preparedness saves several in response. Against: Rapid effective response (search and rescue, medical care, aid) reduces deaths and long-term impacts; some events are too large or sudden for preparedness alone. Conclusion: Preparedness is generally more cost-effective, but effective response and recovery remain essential parts of the hazard management cycle.

items.answer: Hazard maps restrict building in high-risk zones (floodplains, lahar paths, liquefiable land); open spaces as refuges; critical buildings in safe areas.

items.stem: Explain why Japan is a hazardous environment.
items.answer: It lies where four plates meet (Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian, North American): earthquakes, tsunamis and over 100 active volcanoes; typhoons, heavy rain and landslides; dense coastal population.

items.stem: Explain the management of the volcanic hazard on Montserrat.
items.answer: Montserrat Volcano Observatory monitors the volcano; exclusion zone covering the south including the old capital Plymouth; evacuation and resettlement in the north; UK aid for new housing and infrastructure.

items.stem: Using one named example of the management of a hazardous environment, evaluate the success of the management.
items.answer: Bangladesh (tropical cyclones): Deaths fell from about 300 000 (1970) to about 3400 (Sidr 2007) and 26 (Amphan 2020); but losses of homes, crops and land to salinity remain high, shelters can be overcrowded and poor women face barriers to evacuation.

items.stem: Using one named example of the management of a hazardous environment, describe the strategies used to manage the hazards.

items.stem: Explain why management did not prevent large losses in the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami.
items.answer: The tsunami (up to about 40 m locally) overtopped walls designed for smaller events; people relied on walls and earlier warnings underestimated the height; the Fukushima nuclear accident added a technological disaster.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Building codes saved many lives in Japan in 2011.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Few buildings collapsed from shaking despite magnitude 9.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the management of the volcanic hazard on Montserrat. (b) A student writes: “Japan’s management prevented any deaths in 2011.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Montserrat Volcano Observatory monitors the volcano; exclusion zone covering the south including the old capital Plymouth; evacuation and resettlement in the north; UK aid for new housing and infrastructure. (b) Not correct. About 18 000 people died, mostly in the tsunami.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name a case study of the management of a hazardous environment you have studied. For your example, describe the strategies used to manage the hazards.
items.answer: Montserrat (Soufrière Hills volcano): Montserrat Volcano Observatory (1995) monitors seismicity, deformation and gas; exclusion zone and hazard-level system; evacuation of the south including Plymouth; resettlement in the north at Little Bay and Brades; UK aid.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the management of hazardous environments is more successful in HICs than in LICs? In your answer you may refer to governance and economic losses.
items.answer: For: Japan and Chile have strong building codes, monitoring and resources; deaths per event are low. Against: HICs can fail (Katrina 2005, Tōhoku 2011); LICs such as Bangladesh have reduced cyclone deaths dramatically through low-cost community preparedness; economic losses are often higher in HICs. Conclusion: Wealth helps, but effective governance and community preparedness are what make management successful.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Vulnerability can be reduced by development.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A hazard in an uninhabited area is still a disaster.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Better housing, education, health and incomes increase resilience. (b) Not correct. A disaster requires people or property to be affected.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Vulnerability can be reduced by development.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Everyone in a community is equally vulnerable to a hazard.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Better housing, education, health and incomes increase resilience. (b) Not correct. The poor, elderly, disabled, women and children are often more vulnerable.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that vulnerability is more important than the physical hazard in determining the scale of a disaster?
items.answer: For: Similar hazards cause very different losses: Haiti 2010 (M7.0, over 200 000 deaths) vs Christchurch 2011 (M6.2, 185 deaths); PAR model. Against: Extreme magnitude events overwhelm even prepared societies (Tōhoku 2011); the type and speed of onset of the hazard matter; some hazards are inherently deadly. Conclusion: Vulnerability usually explains differences in losses, though very large events cause disasters even where vulnerability is low.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a model showing how quality of life falls during a disaster and recovers through relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction”.
items.answer: Park’s disaster response curve
items.markingKey: Park’s disaster response curve: a model showing how quality of life falls during a disaster and recovers through relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the stages of Park’s disaster response curve. (b) Explain how volcanic eruptions can be predicted.
items.answer: (a) Normal quality of life; the event causes a sharp fall; relief (hours to days: rescue, medical care, aid); rehabilitation (weeks to months: services restored); reconstruction (years), possibly to a better level than before. (b) Monitoring of seismic swarms, ground deformation (tiltmeters, GPS, InSAR), gas emissions (SO₂), temperature changes and past eruption history; allowed the evacuation of over 60 000 people before Pinatubo in 1991.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Prevention of earthquakes is possible.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how land-use planning can reduce hazard impacts.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Earthquakes cannot be prevented; only their effects can be reduced. (b) Hazard maps restrict building in high-risk zones (floodplains, lahar paths, liquefiable land); open spaces as refuges; critical buildings in safe areas.

items.stem: Table 12.2 shows the approximate number of deaths in Bangladesh from four major tropical cyclones: 1970 (Bhola cyclone): about 300 000; 1991 (the 1991 cyclone): about 138 000; 2007 (Cyclone Sidr): about 3 400; 2020 (Cyclone Amphan): about 26. (a) Explain how preparedness has reduced cyclone deaths in Bangladesh. (b) Suggest why deaths are not the only measure of the success of hazard management.
items.answer: (a) The Cyclone Preparedness Programme’s volunteers spread warnings by megaphone and radio; thousands of raised cyclone shelters; evacuation of millions (about 2.4 million before Amphan); embankments and mangrove planting; better forecasting. (b) Economic losses, homes and crops destroyed, people displaced, injuries, salinisation of land and long-term poverty also measure impact.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why management did not prevent large losses in the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. (b) A student writes: “Japan’s management prevented any deaths in 2011.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) The tsunami (up to about 40 m locally) overtopped walls designed for smaller events; people relied on walls and earlier warnings underestimated the height; the Fukushima nuclear accident added a technological disaster. (b) Not correct. About 18 000 people died, mostly in the tsunami.

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the success of the management, for Montserrat (Soufrière Hills volcano) or another example of the management of a hazardous environment.
items.answer: Montserrat (Soufrière Hills volcano): Only 19 deaths, in 1997, among people who had entered the exclusion zone; but the capital, airport and port were destroyed, two-thirds of the people emigrated and the economy depends on UK aid.
